ingredients.name: Roasted rice flour (red or white)
ingredients.notes: approx. 4 cups; use pre-roasted pittu/string-hopper flour, not plain raw rice flour

ingredients.name: Scraped or grated coconut
ingredients.notes: approx. 2.5-3 cups; fresh is best, moistened desiccated coconut works as a substitute

ingredients.name: Water
ingredients.notes: added gradually; exact amount depends on how dry the flour is

steps.instruction: In a large bowl, gently mix the roasted rice flour with the salt.
Add the scraped coconut to the flour and mix to combine evenly.

Sprinkle water into the mixture gradually, working it in with your fingertips in a circular rubbing motion. You are aiming for a crumbly texture, like wet sand or breadcrumbs -- moist but not wet, holding together loosely when pressed without becoming sticky or doughy.
Bring water to a boil in the base of a pittu steamer (or a regular steamer fitted with a bamboo/perforated insert).

Fill the pittu cylinder with the flour-coconut mixture without pressing it down tightly -- a loose fill allows steam to pass through evenly. If using a bamboo colander instead, line it with a clean damp cloth and spread the mixture on top.
Place the filled cylinder onto the steamer base. Steam for about 5-6 minutes, until you see steam coming through the top of the pittu and it is firm to the touch.
Push the cooked pittu out of the cylinder using a wooden dowel or the back of a spoon. Repeat with the remaining mixture in batches.
Serve warm with warmed coconut milk (lightly salted), lunu miris, or any spicy meat, fish, or vegetable curry.

source_site: elanka.com.au, cross-checked against rasakama.wordpress.com and toneandtaste.com for technique and ratio consistency
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 3 independent sources for consistent flour-to-coconut ratio and crumb texture description
notes: Pittu (puttu in South India) is traditionally made in a cylindrical bamboo or metal steamer called a 'pittu bambuwa'. The crumbly texture of the dough -- not a wet dough -- is the single most important technique point; over-wetting produces a dense, gummy result rather than the airy steamed texture pittu is known for. Variations include kurakkan (finger millet) flour pittu, served simply with coconut and jaggery rather than savoury curries.
